role: reference-only: pre-pilot source records for quote and provenance comparison

t1-l01-oral-tradition.title: Source A
t1-l01-oral-tradition.extract: The Creator’s teachings are reinforced through the oral tradition, which is the collection of spoken words that pass down a culture’s teachings from generation to generation.
t1-l01-oral-tradition.creator: Contemporary Issues textbook authors
t1-l01-oral-tradition.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.contextLimits: The authors’ definition, in a passage on traditional First Nations worldviews — not a quotation from a storyteller.

t1-l01-oral-tradition.title: Source B
t1-l01-oral-tradition.extract: The following is a creation story of the Nehiyawak, who are also known as the Cree. Kayas*, all the creatures that walked, flew, crawled and slithered lived peacefully together on Turtle Island. (Turtle Island was the name for North America, because it sat on the back of a giant turtle.)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.creator: Nehiyawak (Cree) telling, as presented in the course reading
t1-l01-oral-tradition.locator: Walking Together reading (Indigenous Canada, Module 1), printed p. 5 (file p. 8)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.attribution: Indigenous Canada course materials, University of Alberta, via the course reading
t1-l01-oral-tradition.contextLimits: One printed telling; the reading notes that many versions of this story exist. The asterisk marks a reading note. No single teller is named on the page.

t1-l01-oral-tradition.title: Source C
t1-l01-oral-tradition.extract: If the legends fall silent, who will teach the children of our ways?
t1-l01-oral-tradition.speaker: Chief Dan George
t1-l01-oral-tradition.date: 1974, as cited in the course reading
t1-l01-oral-tradition.creator: Chief Dan George, as quoted in the course reading
t1-l01-oral-tradition.locator: Walking Together reading (Indigenous Canada, Module 1), printed p. 4 (file p. 7)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.attribution: Indigenous Canada course materials, University of Alberta, via the course reading
t1-l01-oral-tradition.contextLimits: A dated quotation from a named speaker. The page gives no community label for the speaker, so the lesson names none.

t1-l01-oral-tradition.title: Source D
t1-l01-oral-tradition.extract: They work to instruct and educate on how to behave properly. They also act as guides for how to live and engage with the world.
t1-l01-oral-tradition.creator: Indigenous Canada course authors, citing Kovach (2010)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.locator: Walking Together reading (Indigenous Canada, Module 1), printed p. 7 (file p. 10)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.attribution: Indigenous Canada course materials, University of Alberta, via the course reading
t1-l01-oral-tradition.contextLimits: The authors’ summary of how stories function, with a cited source — not a storyteller’s own words.

t1-l01-oral-tradition.title: Source E
t1-l01-oral-tradition.extract: Each nation has a creation story and its own distinct oral tradition. There are four general components of storytelling for Indigenous peoples: connection between generations; acknowledging change over generations; moral guide and social mechanisms; and transmission of history and culture (Dumbrill and Green 2008).
t1-l01-oral-tradition.creator: Indigenous Canada course authors, citing Dumbrill and Green (2008)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.locator: Walking Together reading (Indigenous Canada, Module 1), printed p. 7 (file p. 10)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.attribution: Indigenous Canada course materials, University of Alberta, via the course reading
t1-l01-oral-tradition.contextLimits: A cited scholarly summary. The first sentence is the direct answer to the one-tradition misconception.

t1-l01-oral-tradition.title: Source F
t1-l01-oral-tradition.extract: For example, the Supreme Court has ruled that oral history regarding land use and governance should be given as much consideration as written evidence when making decisions about Aboriginal rights.
t1-l01-oral-tradition.creator: Contemporary Issues textbook authors
t1-l01-oral-tradition.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l01-oral-tradition.contextLimits: The authors’ report of a court ruling about decisions on Aboriginal rights — not a claim that every telling decides every case. The same pages discuss Mushkegowuk Cree Elder James Carpenter’s testimony.

t1-l02-nations-peoples.title: Source A
t1-l02-nations-peoples.extract: We the Dene of the N.W.T . insist on the right to be regarded by ourselves and the world as a Nation.
t1-l02-nations-peoples.speaker: The Dene, in the 1975 Dene Declaration
t1-l02-nations-peoples.creator: Indian Brotherhood of the Northwest Territories (now the Dene Nation)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.contextLimits: A 1975 political assertion; spelling and punctuation reproduce the original at the Dene Nation’s request. Read as a dated statement.

t1-l02-nations-peoples.title: Source B
t1-l02-nations-peoples.extract: Other peoples who have occupied the land — often with force — and foreign governments have imposed themselves on our people. Ancient civilizations and ways of life have been destroyed.
t1-l02-nations-peoples.speaker: The Dene, in the 1975 Dene Declaration
t1-l02-nations-peoples.creator: Indian Brotherhood of the Northwest Territories (now the Dene Nation)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.contextLimits: The Declaration’s own account of colonization, in its own words — including “often with force” and “destroyed.”

t1-l02-nations-peoples.title: Source C
t1-l02-nations-peoples.extract: While the Native people of Canada are a minority in their homeland, the Native people of the N.W.T ., the Dene and the Inuit, are a majority of the population of the N.W.T .
t1-l02-nations-peoples.speaker: The Dene, in the 1975 Dene Declaration
t1-l02-nations-peoples.creator: Indian Brotherhood of the Northwest Territories (now the Dene Nation)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.contextLimits: A 1975 population statement. It describes the Declaration’s own time; it does not automatically describe the territory today.

t1-l02-nations-peoples.title: Source E
t1-l02-nations-peoples.extract: The Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) word for the concept of nation, kanakerahsera, has the root naker, which means “to be born.”
t1-l02-nations-peoples.creator: Contemporary Issues textbook authors
t1-l02-nations-peoples.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.contextLimits: The authors’ language example: Haudenosaunee and English both root nation in birth. The surrounding passage gives the Latin parallel.

t1-l02-nations-peoples.title: Source F
t1-l02-nations-peoples.extract: The word nation is sometimes used interchangeably with the word people. Used in this way, people is not the plural of person, referring to a group of individuals. In this special meaning, people is the group as a whole.
t1-l02-nations-peoples.creator: Contemporary Issues textbook authors
t1-l02-nations-peoples.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.contextLimits: A terminology distinction, not a legal ruling. The passage adds that a people has special rights recognized by international law.

t1-l02-nations-peoples.title: Source D1
t1-l02-nations-peoples.extract: What we the Dene are struggling for is the recognition of the Dene Nation by the governments and peoples of the world.
t1-l02-nations-peoples.speaker: The Dene, in the 1975 Dene Declaration
t1-l02-nations-peoples.creator: Indian Brotherhood of the Northwest Territories (now the Dene Nation)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.contextLimits: The Declaration’s own statement of its struggle — recognition of the Dene Nation.

t1-l02-nations-peoples.title: Source D2
t1-l02-nations-peoples.extract: What we seek then is independence and self-determination within the country of Canada. This is what we mean when we call for a just land settlement for the Dene Nation.
t1-l02-nations-peoples.speaker: The Dene, in the 1975 Dene Declaration
t1-l02-nations-peoples.creator: Indian Brotherhood of the Northwest Territories (now the Dene Nation)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t1-l02-nations-peoples.contextLimits: The Declaration’s own definition of a just land settlement: independence and self-determination within Canada.

t2-l01-why-land-matters.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t2-l01-why-land-matters.contextLimits: The wardship sentence, beginning after a print-spacing break ('A triumph because, under the Treaty, we ...'). What ends: wardship and beggary in the Nisga'a's own lands.
t2-l01-why-land-matters.creator: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.extract: will no longer be wards of the state, no longer beggars in our own lands
t2-l01-why-land-matters.speaker: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.title: Source A

t2-l01-why-land-matters.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t2-l01-why-land-matters.contextLimits: The ownership clause, ending before the postage-stamp comparison line. What begins: collective ownership of the land base.
t2-l01-why-land-matters.creator: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.extract: will collectively own about 2000 square kilometres of land
t2-l01-why-land-matters.speaker: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.title: Source B

t2-l01-why-land-matters.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t2-l01-why-land-matters.contextLimits: The self-government clause in full. Note the boundary Gosnell sets: own institutions, within Canadian law.
t2-l01-why-land-matters.creator: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.extract: We will once again govern ourselves by our own institutions, but within the context of Canadian law.
t2-l01-why-land-matters.speaker: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.title: Source C

t2-l01-why-land-matters.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t2-l01-why-land-matters.contextLimits: The Question 1 answer sentence, beginning after a print-spacing break ('A triumph because, clause by clause, the Nisga'a Treaty ...'). Three nouns — memorize all three.
t2-l01-why-land-matters.creator: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.extract: emphasizes self-reliance, personal responsibility, and modern education
t2-l01-why-land-matters.speaker: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.title: Source D

t2-l01-why-land-matters.attribution: Contemporary Issues: Aboriginal Studies 30 (Les Éditions Duval, 2005)
t2-l01-why-land-matters.contextLimits: The treaty's definition, beginning after a print-spacing break ('To us, ...'). Gosnell defines treaty by relationship, not by paperwork.
t2-l01-why-land-matters.creator: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.extract: a treaty is a sacred instrument. It represents an understanding between distinct cultures and shows respect for each other's way of life.
t2-l01-why-land-matters.speaker: Dr. Joseph Gosnell
t2-l01-why-land-matters.title: Source E
